analysis.one_liner: Raises the minimum wage modestly while cutting small business, pension, and estate taxes.
analysis.headline: The House passed a scaled-back minimum wage increase bundled with business and estate tax cuts 257-169 on March 9, 2000, but the Senate never voted and the federal minimum wage stayed at $5.15.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.65 in 2000 and $6.15 in 2001, and paired that with a long list of tax benefits: full health-insurance deductions for the self-employed, higher small-business expensing, larger meal deductions, expanded retirement-savings limits, estate tax rate cuts for large estates, and new tax incentives for low-income communities. When it reached the House floor, a rules change swapped in a smaller, slower wage increase than the tax committee had approved, and added new overtime exemptions. The House passed it 257-169, but the Senate never brought it to a vote, so no wage increase passed and the tax cuts never happened either.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had become law: minimum-wage workers would get two wage increases (to $5.65 in 2000, $6.15 in 2001) [S4]; self-employed people would deduct 100% of health insurance costs [S4]; workers 50 and older could make extra retirement contributions and employer matching contributions would vest faster [S4]; small businesses would get higher expensing and meal deductions [S4]; owners of large estates would pay lower estate tax rates with a top rate of 50% above $2.5 million [S4]; residents of designated poor areas would get capital-gains and savings-account tax breaks [S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers, small businesses, wealthy estates

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.65 beginning April 2000 and to $6.15 beginning April 2001, the first increase since 1997.
Requires faster vesting of employer matching contributions, cutting the cliff vesting period from 5 years to 3 so workers keep their match sooner.
Lets workers age 50 and older make additional catch-up retirement contributions and raises the limits on 401(k) deferrals and pension contributions.
Allows retirement savings to be rolled among 401(k), 403(b), and government 457 plans, making it easier to carry savings between jobs.
Lets self-employed people deduct 100% of their family's health insurance costs and raises small-business expensing to $30,000.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury bears the cost of the tax cuts, including lower estate tax rates on estates over $2.5 million. Businesses that employ minimum-wage workers bear the higher payroll costs, and some salaried workers (computer professionals, certain commissioned sales employees, funeral directors) would lose overtime protections.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal Treasury, minimum-wage employers, some salaried workers

drawbacks.text: The wage increase is smaller and slower than what the Ways and Means Committee had approved: the committee bill reached $5.48 in 2000, $5.81 in 2001, and $6.15 in 2002 over three steps, while the floor version reached $5.65 in 2000 and $6.15 in 2001 in two steps, and the first step came six months later.

The bill exempts certain computer professionals, specialized commissioned sales employees, and licensed funeral directors and embalmers from minimum wage and overtime requirements, removing protections from specific groups of workers.
The estate tax provisions cut the top rate and raise the exemption toward $1 million, concentrating tax relief on the largest estates and reducing federal revenue.

Raising pension contribution limits ($160,000 defined-benefit cap, $40,000 defined-contribution cap, $200,000 compensation cap) disproportionately benefits workers and owners who can afford to defer large amounts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill contains a real, though modest, minimum wage increase and genuinely worker-friendly pension changes such as faster vesting and easier rollovers. But the wage increase attached to it was weaker than the committee's own version, and the price of getting it included large tax cuts skewed toward businesses and the biggest estates, plus new overtime exemptions for some workers. An honest supporter would acknowledge that this was a trade: a smaller pay raise for millions of workers in exchange for tax relief aimed at businesses and wealthy estates.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 257-169 after a rule swapped in a smaller wage increase, but the Senate placed it on its calendar and never voted; when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001 the bill died and the minimum wage stayed at $5.15.

narrative.text: Introduced October 14, 1999 as the Wage and Employment Growth Act, the original bill phased the minimum wage from $5.15 to $6.15 over three steps ending April 2002, alongside small-business, pension, and estate tax provisions.

The Ways and Means Committee ordered it reported amended on a 23-14 vote on November 9, 1999, and the Education and Workforce Committee held it under extensions until being discharged in January 2000.

On March 8-9, 2000, the Rules Committee's rule replaced the committee bill's text with that of H.R. 3832, which contained a smaller two-step wage increase ($5.65 then $6.15) plus new overtime exemptions, and attached H.R. 3846.

Representative Charles Rangel moved to recommit the bill with instructions, a last attempt to change it before the final vote; it failed 207-218, with 205 of 211 Democrats supporting it and only 1 of 221 Republicans.
The House passed the bill 257-169: 215 of 222 Republicans voted yes while only 41 of 211 Democrats did.

The Senate received the bill in March 2000, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 468; no committee action, debate, or vote ever followed before Congress ended January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage workers came out ahead, because the wage stayed at $5.15 for years after the bill died; the tax-cut provisions also never took effect, so no one gained those. Workers got no raise, and the estate and business tax cuts never materialized either.

sides.party_line_note: Both votes split sharply by party: the motion to recommit failed 207-218 with 205 of 211 Democrats in favor and only 1 of 221 Republicans, and final passage passed 257-169 with 215 of 222 Republicans yes against 41 of 211 Democrats.

industries.note: The bill repeals the two highest estate tax brackets, sets a 50% top rate on estates over $2.5 million, and replaces the credit with an exemption rising to $1 million, a first step toward full repeal. The revenue cost falls on the general Treasury rather than on the estates themselves.

They gain a 100% health-insurance deduction, $30,000 expensing, larger meal deductions, income averaging for fishermen, and repeal of liquor occupational taxes. They also absorb the higher cost of a minimum wage increase, which is why wage and tax provisions were bundled together.

Higher contribution limits, catch-up contributions, and expanded rollovers among 401(k), 403(b), and 457 plans push more retirement money through privately managed accounts and their administrators. Workers benefit from the same provisions, so the industry's interest runs alongside savers' here.

The wage increase raises their labor costs, offset for them by the bill's higher business meal deductions. Their interest in diluting or delaying the wage increase runs against the workers who would get the raise.
New exemptions from minimum wage and overtime rules for computer professionals and certain commissioned sales employees reduce their payroll obligations directly at some workers' expense.

industries.industry: Real estate and low-income housing developers
industries.note: The bill expands the low-income housing credit ceiling and eases REIT tax rules, channeling more public support for affordable housing through tax-credit investors and developers. It also excludes forgiven mortgage debt from income, helping distressed homeowners.
